newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Lisbon sees Nobel Peace award pressuring Jakarta.
newsitem.headline: Lisbon sees Nobel Peace award pressuring Jakarta.

text.p: Portugal reacted with delight on Friday to the award of the Nobel Peace Prize to two leading defenders of human rights in East Timor, saying it could push Indonesia into easing its iron grip over Lisbon's former colony.
The Lisbon government has been locked in largely fruitless negotiations with Jakarta over the future of the territory, invaded and annexed with great loss of life two decades ago.

Portuguese leaders said that the awarding of the $1.2-million prize to Carlos Filipe Ximenes Belo, Roman Catholic Bishop of Dili, East Timor's capital, and exiled resistance leader Jose Ramos-Horta could help unblock the situation.
"I hope that these proofs of the interest of the international community will make things change and make Indonesia finally move," Prime Minister Antonio Guterres told Reuters.
But Indonesia reacted negatively to the award, calling one of the prize-winners a "political opportunist" and avoiding all comment on the other.
The opportunist jibe appeared aimed at Ramos-Horta, the international spokesman for jailed resistance leader Xanana Gusmao who was captured by Indonesian forces in 1992.

The issue of East Timor has become a thorn in the side of relations between the emerging economic powerhouses of the Far East, of which Indonesia is a leading member, and the European Union (EU), with Portugal rarely letting an opportunity pass to bring the matter up in international forums.
Guterres had appealed to Indonesia's President Suharto to break the diplomatic deadlock over East Timor at a summit meeting between European and Asian leaders in March in Bangkok.

He offered a step-by-step approach to build bridges between Lisbon and Jakarta, which currently have no diplomatic ties. The proposal, which included the opening of "interest sections" in friendly embassies, was spurned.
Human rights activists say up to 200,000 people died in the Indonesian military invasion of 1975 and the subsequent military crackdown and a famine.

Indonesia's annexation of the territory the following year has never been recognised by the United Nations, which has brokered several rounds of talks between Jakarta and Lisbon since fresh trouble broke out in the territory in 1991.

Clashes are periodically reported between a small guerrilla movement still active in the mountains and the Indonesian army. Street demonstrations and embassy invasions by asylum seekers have kept the international spotlight on the troubled territory.
Through all the talks, Indonesia has stuck to its position that East Timor, which is predominantly Catholic while Indonesia is Moslem, forms part of its territory.
Portugal backs the resistance movement in its demand that the East Timorese be given the chance to decide their own future.
President Jorge Sampaio, and his predecessor Mario Soares, were among leading figures to express their satisfaction at the decision by the Norwegian Nobel Committee in Oslo.
"I am very pleased by the news. It is a wonderful surprise," Sampaio said. "The award reflects their indefatigable work in the service of human rights and peace in the territory," he told reporters.
